steps.headline: Which piece of the Home page should I work on next?
steps.today: Five things you asked for are not built yet: Sonos grouping, search, ticking several devices at once in Edit, a page for each device (its history and maker/model), and a home-wide activity list.
steps.problem: You asked to SEE designs for the device page and the activity list before I build them, so those two need drawings first. The other three are already decided and can be built straight away.
steps.proposal: Pick where to start. Everything else follows after, in the order shown in the recommended option.

options.label: Designs first
options.summary: Draw 2–3 versions each of the device page and the activity list, then build Sonos grouping, search and multi-select while you decide.
pros: You get pictures to choose from soon, and building carries on while you think.
The device page and activity list share a lot (history appears in both), so designing them together avoids building one twice.
cons: Nothing new to tap on the Home page until the first build lands after the deck.

options.label: Sonos grouping first
options.summary: Build the Group button with a tick list of your other Sonos speakers, then the rest.
pros: The feature you were most excited about arrives first.
Already decided, so no deck before it works.
cons: The two designs you asked to see wait longer.

options.label: Search and multi-select first
options.summary: Build search across all devices, and ticking several devices in Edit to hide, move or star them together.
pros: Makes tidying up your many devices much faster right away.
cons: Less exciting day to day once your rooms are tidied.

steps.path: Every card on the Home page
steps.headline: How quickly should the Home page notice changes made somewhere else?
steps.today: The page asks Home Assistant for news every 5 seconds. If someone turns on a light with a switch or the Google app, the card catches up within 5 seconds. Your own taps on the page show instantly.
steps.problem: Up to 5 seconds of a card showing the wrong thing feels slow next to Google Home or Apple Home, which update the moment something changes.
steps.proposal: Three speeds. Each costs a different amount of work.

options.label: Instant
options.summary: The page keeps one line open to Home Assistant, and Home Assistant tells it the moment anything changes.
pros: Feels like a real smart-home app: cards change the same moment the light does.
Actually asks Home Assistant LESS often than checking every few seconds.
cons: The biggest job: the app itself has to learn to keep a line open, plus tests for when the Pi restarts or Wi-Fi drops.
Until that is done well, a dropped line could leave cards frozen — I would show a small 'reconnecting' note if that happens.

options.label: Every 2 seconds
pros: A small change I can make in minutes.
Cards are at most 2 seconds behind.
cons: Asks the Pi 2.5 times as often, which is fine for the Pi but wasteful.

options.label: Keep 5 seconds
cons: The lag you can see today stays.

steps.headline: Should light brightness bars be as tall as the new volume bars?
steps.today: Light brightness bars are thin; the volume bars on speakers and TVs are taller and easier to grab.
steps.problem: Two kinds of sliders on one page look mismatched, and the thin one is harder to drag on a touchscreen.
steps.proposal: Yes makes every light's bar the same height as the volume bar. Rooms with many lights would get a bit longer. No leaves them thin.

steps.path: The Home Assistant website, opened from the Problems page or the Open links
steps.headline: Should Home Assistant's own screens use YouCoded's colours?
steps.today: When a fix button sends you into Home Assistant itself, it uses Home Assistant's default blue look, which looks nothing like YouCoded.
steps.problem: Jumping between the two looks like jumping between two unrelated apps. You said earlier you'd like 'colours at a minimum' to match.
steps.proposal: Yes: I make a Home Assistant colour theme matching your YouCoded theme, and set it as its default. Put WHICH YouCoded theme you use most in the note. No: Home Assistant keeps its own look.

steps.headline: Do the camera cards still look broken to you?
steps.today: Nest cameras now show a note saying Nest needs you to sign in again in Home Assistant, with a button to do it, instead of a black box. The Pi Zero camera shows its picture.
steps.problem: You said 'camera previews are broken'. On your real data I could only find the Nest sign-in cause, so if you saw something else I have not fixed it.
steps.proposal: Yes: describe what you see in the note (or paste a screenshot path), and I'll dig in. No: the Nest sign-in note covers it.

steps.headline: What should happen to the helper's stricter version of the flaky approval test?
steps.today: A test that clicks 'Approve' on a permission request used to fail at random. It is already fixed on the main copy of the app. A helper also wrote a stricter version of that test, saved on its own branch, plus an empty work folder it never used.
steps.problem: The stricter version is optional, and the empty folder is clutter on this computer.
steps.proposal: Choose what to keep. Nothing here changes the app you use.

options.label: Keep it, tidy up
options.summary: Keep the stricter test saved on GitHub for later; delete the empty folder.
pros: Nothing useful is lost, and the clutter goes.
cons: One more saved branch to decide about later.

options.label: Throw both away
pros: Fully tidy; the existing fix already stops the random failures.
cons: The stricter check is gone; it would catch a future break a little sooner.

options.label: Leave everything
cons: The empty folder stays as clutter.

steps.headline: May I restart the test copy of YouCoded now?
steps.today: The test window you try the Home page in is running older app code than what is saved now.
steps.problem: Until it restarts, it lacks the latest fixes from the main app (including the remote-flicker fix being combined with them).
steps.proposal: Yes: I close and reopen ONLY the test window (your everyday YouCoded is not touched). It takes about a minute; anything open in the test window closes. No: I leave it until you say.
